prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned body of Romanian-language prose, with poetry as its foundation, that turns memory, the body and dream into an inner cosmology

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged: Cărtărescu (B011), as a single credited name in one prize part. The citation wording has changed. After the exchange I would make it prose-centred and name the poetry as the foundation of the oeuvre, not as co-equal weight. Carlberg, Sem-Sandberg and Sward argued for this, and it matches my own round-1 condition that the citation should rest on prose alone if the poetry cannot be shown to carry real weight. Nobody in round 1 supplied concrete evidence on the poetry, so I cannot claim more for it than my thin knowledge supports. The literary case remains the one I made earlier. The voice is unmistakably his own. The public record of the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding is its first volume) and of Solenoid points to a metaphysical project built from memory, the body and dream, and to formal ambition at large scale. As I understand the public description, Solenoid is a separate large construction and not a continuation of Orbitor. That is why I read the late work as extension rather than repetition. I hold this as a judgment from public knowledge, not a verified finding. The mature oeuvre can be assessed now, and attribution is clean: one writer, one language, no need to stretch generic categories. I do not count the unanimity of the opening rankings as merit. Its only function is to make the burden of testing the case heavier on us.
statement.case_against: The reservations are unresolved, and discussion alone cannot resolve them. First, much of the achievement lies in Romanian rhythm, syntax and density, so we judge it indirectly. Second, maximalism may conceal unevenness in the later long novels. Third, my knowledge of the poetry and early work is thinner than my knowledge of the major prose, and nobody in round 1 improved it. If anonymous Romanian-reading expert reports, which the committee has used for other literatures, indicated that the sentence-level surface is overrated in translation, or that the later volumes enlarge without advancing, the case would weaken materially. Adonis would then be the stronger alternative, because the remaking of a whole poetic language is the central question there. Carson would be the alternative if inventiveness of form is weighted above scale. I also record a bias risk. My own scholarship is in modern poetry, the fragment and exile literature, and the poetry candidates I ranked highly (Adonis, Zurita) sit close to that field. I therefore hold them to the same standard of argument from the poems as the others, and I have not carried Zurita as an alternative because that argument has not been made.

responses.point: Carlberg revised her opening so that the poetry is named in the citation but does not carry the award, and she asks that the late-volume claim stay an open question. She keeps Adonis as a strong alternative but not a firm first choice, because Arabic prosody and diction are hard to judge in selective translation.
responses.response: I accept the prose-centred wording and have adopted it in my citation. I agree that the late-volume claim is the crux and should stay open, so I do not offer it as a finding. On Adonis we are close. He is my first alternative, and I would argue him from the poems. The essays and his public positions are context only. But a recommendation resting on prosody that neither of us can assess directly is weaker than one resting on prose whose architecture is visible in translation. A stronger Arabic-reading expert report is what would change that, not further ranking. I would ask Carlberg, as the member who ranked him second, to name which collections she would put forward on the poems alone.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg accepts that the late work extends the project but only provisionally, and he would not rest the citation on any single late novel. He argues the case should be the cumulative, recognisable structure of the whole, with the unverified quality across volumes stated openly. He also suggests Romanian readers or the Swedish translations could reduce the translation uncertainty more than further ranking would.
responses.response: I agree with all of this, including the correction to how I put the claim. My statement that the late work extends the earlier project is a reading from public knowledge, not a verified finding, and the citation should not depend on any one late book. His proposal on the translation limit is the most practical way forward. I would add that a Romanian reader's report should be asked about specific features: whether density in the sentences is controlled, and whether register and pacing hold across long stretches. A general verdict of admiration would not answer that. If such a report found loss of control in the late volumes, I would shift weight toward the strongest earlier works in the citation instead of dropping the laureate.

responses.point: Mattson treats extension rather than repetition as the right test and the basis of her confidence in maturity. She also says unevenness is a question for close reading of the later volumes, not something the opening rankings have settled. She differs with me on Zurita because the written poetry must carry the case and she cannot judge it in translation.
responses.response: On the test we agree, and I find her insistence on close reading of the later volumes the right discipline. I asked in round 1 that length be separated from loss of control. In practice I would look for formal development: whether later sections introduce new structure, register or perspective, or return to earlier effects with less pressure. I cannot supply that reading myself from public knowledge alone. On Zurita I concede her point. I ranked him fourth in the opening, but I cannot show from the written poems that his sequences hold in translation, and the memorial and landscape dimension cannot substitute for that evidence. I have therefore not carried him among my two alternatives. This is a difference of evidence, not of principle.

responses.point: Palm treats the classification problem for Carson as a drafting difficulty more than a literary weakness, but concedes that it makes her a less secure single-writer citation than Cărtărescu. She also says that Can Xue's sustained method is a real strength of voice, while its development over time is unanswered.
responses.response: I accept her distinction. What counts as Carson's oeuvre is a drafting question, and it should not be mistaken for a defect in Autobiography of Red or Nox. I would still treat that drafting problem as bearing on a recommendation, because a citation must say what it honours. A defensible Carson citation would name her original verse, hybrid and essayistic work and set aside translations and adaptations, and I am not sure the remaining body of work supports the sustained quality the criteria ask for. That keeps her as my second alternative, not as a rival to B011. On Can Xue, Palm and I agree on the originality of the voice. Neither of us has named a specific work or period where the dream-logic mode deepens, and until someone does I cannot move her above my current ordering.

uncertainties: Whether Cărtărescu's sentence-level achievement in Romanian survives translation cannot be settled from the translated corpus or my public knowledge. Romanian-reading expert reports would be the proper test.

Whether the later volumes of the multi-part works and Solenoid advance the project or only enlarge it is my judgment from public knowledge, not verified reading, and remains the central open question on sustained quality.
The weight of the poetry and early work is unestablished. The citation therefore treats prose as the centre and poetry as foundation.

For Adonis, Carson, Can Xue, Tawada and Zurita, translation or corpus-definition limits mean that comparisons with Cărtărescu rest on incomplete evidence. A different level of access could change the ordering.

No source in the supplied record establishes Carlberg's committee voting status, so the six-vote model is a modelling assumption. The unanimity of round 1 has not been tested by a sustained counter-case and is not evidence of merit.
statement.conflict_note: No documented connection to any shortlisted writer appears in my supplied profile. Documented ties are to Horace Engdahl, Daniel Birnbaum and the Kris circle, and to committee colleagues, none of which involves a candidate. My scholarship in modern poetry, the fragment and exile literature, and my translation of Celan, are context only and not evidence of preference. I have disclosed that my opening ranks of Adonis (third) and Zurita (fourth) sit close to that field, and I apply the same standard of argument from the texts to them as to prose candidates. As chair I have not adjudicated any conflict, and no recusal is proposed on the supplied evidence.
